To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

dogs and foxes have supplanted raptors as the principal scavengers on urban beaches and have become the dominant scavengers in coastal reserves, with potentially serious consequences for the conservation of native scavengers and scavenging raptors.
dogs are ubiquitous and abundant on beaches and dunes, and are the most important scavengers on beaches, displacing native species.

small coastal reserves in urbanized landscapes can support abundant populations of domestic dogs that are functionally important scavengers and that may compromise the conservation objectives of the reserve.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the conservation of small, coastal reserves, and how they function as effective conservation areas in the face of the impacts of non-native canids, particularly dogs.
the ecological effects of urbanization on small coastal reserves, with a focus on the impacts of domestic canids.
the ecological effects of domestic dogs in small, protected reserves, and their potential to compromise the functional conservation of these reserves.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
small conservation areas, in the face of urban development, may not always be able to function as intended, even when the conservation area is legally protected.
the presence of dogs on beaches has a negative impact on the ecosystem.
dogs have effectively taken over the role of scavengers in these small reserves, and are likely to do so in others of this type, unless they can be controlled.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
conservation of coastal dunes in urbanized landscapes requires management of both native and non-native scavengers, and in particular, management of the most abundant non-native scavengers.

the ecological integrity of small, coastal reserves is threatened by the presence of domestic dogs and red foxes, and that the ecological integrity and conservation value of small, coastal conservation areas is compromised by their inability to exclude domestic dogs and red-foxes, even in the face of intensive fox-control programs.

, on urbanized beaches, small conservation reserves can continue to be effective conservation instruments, but that they must be managed to control non-native canids, especially domestic dogs, which have become the dominant scavengers on the dune-beach interface, and are a key threat to native scavengers and scavenger guild function.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the ecological integrity and function of small coastal reserves can be compromised by domestic dogs.

, in the context of urbanized coastlines, the ecological integrity of small conservation areas is compromised by domestic dogs and that, to maintain ecosystem function, dogs should be managed to the same level as foxes in such reserves.

, in the face of increasing human encroachment on coastal ecosystems and their associated biodiversity, conservation of coastal areas will be more difficult to achieve without a concerted effort to manage the human impacts that threaten them.
